title: VPC Edge Proxy Translation & Firewall Tiering — Playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working playbook for hardening and operationalizing edge egress/proxy translation and a three-tier firewall model for Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem) deployments. Focus is on:
- deterministic egress behavior (SNAT/translation) for customer traffic
- clear firewall tiers (edge/transit/workload) and responsibilities
- proxy-based allowlist + transparent failover pattern
- Terraform module layout and an upgrade plan with smoke tests and rollback criteria

Audience:
Solutions engineers, platform SREs, infra engineers responsible for private deployments, and the on-call rotations that will operate upgrades.

Context / motivation (short):
Customers want predictable outbound IPs for allowlisting, strong ingress/egress controls, and a disaster-resilient proxy path. Previous on-prem installs exhibited: occasional TTL-related DNS inconsistencies when traffic crossed VXLAN tunnels, and opaque failure modes when an edge proxy was overloaded. This playbook proposes a repeatable architecture and an upgrade path for Terraform modules we maintain in terraform-modules/private-networking.

High-level architecture (proposed):
- Edge (boundary) layer: per-region/static egress nodes that run the edge-proxy (forward proxy + translation). These nodes are the only systems allowed to SNAT customer traffic to external destinations. They perform TLS inspection hooks (optional), header enrichment, and consistent public IP allocation (for allowlists).
- Transit layer: fast path routers / BGP peers or cloud route tables that carry traffic between on-prem/VPC and edge nodes. Controls here are coarse ACLs limiting destinations by CIDR and port ranges to reduce blast radius.
- Workload (pod/host) layer: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies + host-level iptables/eBPF to prevent lateral movement and to ensure traffic destined for external systems is routed to the local gateway (not directly to internet).

Key design decisions and rationale:
1) Centralized SNAT at edge nodes vs. decentralized NAT on customer gateways:
   - Centralized SNAT (recommended): single or small set of stable public IPs per region simplifies allowlisting for customers and auditing. Costs: slightly higher egress hop, requires HA and scaling. Benefits: predictable origin IP, unified proxy policies and observability.
   - Decentralized SNAT: lower egress latency for on-prem local egress, but harder to manage and to provide predictable outbound IPs.

2) Proxy mode: explicit forward proxy + transparent intercept (auto-config) for legacy workloads.
   - Default = forward proxy + iptables redirection on gateway nodes for egress.
   - Transparent mode allowed for environments where changing application configs is infeasible, but increases complexity (ssl-bump concerns, certs).

3) Failover model: N edge proxies per region behind an anycast/route-based failover or using a region-local VIP with health checks.
   - Prefer DNS+Health-check small TTL (30s) for cloud-managed customers.
   - For on-prem customers using BGP, announce best path from active proxies and withdraw on failure.

4) Firewall tiering:
   - Edge tier: Stateful firewall rules limiting outbound ports, rate limits, and proxy listener controls. Managed by Redwood but configurable per-customer via policy templates.
   - Transit tier: route-based controls and coarse packet filters (deny by default, allow specific transit subnets). Owned jointly with customer netops for on-prem.
   - Workload tier: namespaced NetworkPolicies (default deny) and annotation-driven egress rules (managed by customer).

Operational controls and SLOs:
- Proxy availability: 99.95% per region. Alert on >2 concurrent proxy failures or >5% 5m error-rate.
- Egress latency: P50 < 20ms additional for regional workloads; P95 < 80ms.
- DNS resolution error rate for private DNS: <0.1% per hour.
- Origin IP consistency: audit log shows <1 config drift per week.

Terraform module notes (layout + recommended interfaces):
Module: terraform-modules/private-edge-proxy 
- inputs (string list): region, vpc_id, subnet_ids, allowed_eips, instance_count_min, instance_count_max, proxy_image_tag, logging_bucket, healthcheck_path
- outputs (string list): edge_vip, egress_ips, proxy_asg_name, cloudwatch_log_group (or equivalent)
- resources: autoscaling group | managed instance group, target group, route table updates, cloud NAT fallback (if enabled)
- recommended versioning: semver with major bump for network/TLS behavior changes (v1.0.0 -> v2.0.0 when switching SNAT mode or TLS-intercept), keep changelog in GH releases

Module: terraform-modules/private-firewall-tiering
- inputs: policy_templates (map), transit_acl_rules (list), workload_default_policy (string: deny|allow), audit_log_bucket
- outputs: edge_policy_id, transit_acl_id, workload_policy_annotation_key
- notes: avoid embedding customer CIDRs in module itself — expose variables so customer-specific TF can pass values.

Module upgrade guidance (major points):
- Always branch per-customer (customer-<id>/upgrade-edge-<version>).
- Validate in staging with exact same CIDR & MTU as customer prod (common failure cause).
- Use canary: pick a low-traffic customer or single availability zone. Deploy new module version with new resource names where possible (blue/green) to avoid destructive changes.
- Smoke tests (automated): outbound HTTP to 3x public endpoints, DNS resolution for internal service names, verify egress IPs match expected list, run a penetration-lite scan to ensure ports blocked.
- Rollback triggers: 5xx traffic increase >3% over baseline for 10m, DNS error spike >0.5% sustained for 5m, operator-logged connectivity failures.

Concrete terraform snippet examples (person working notes):
- edge proxy autoscaling flavour (pseudo-TF):
  module "edge_proxy" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//private-edge-proxy?ref=v1.3.0"
    region = var.region
    vpc_id = module.vpc.id
    subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnets
    allowed_eips = var.edge_static_ips
    proxy_image_tag = var.proxy_image_tag
    instance_count_min = 2
    instance_count_max = 6
  }

- note on stateful updates: prefer replacing ASG instances rather than in-place instance-type changes for kernel-level eBPF programs that might change MTU behavior.

DNS implications and private resolution patterns:
- Use CoreDNS (k8s) for internal service discovery. For external name resolution and split-horizon needs, configure conditional forwarding on edge DNS servers:
  - forward cloud-resolver (10.0.0.2) for public-record lookups
  - stub domain for "svc.customer.local" to local on-prem resolvers to preserve local answers
- TTL policy: keep low TTL (30–60s) for edge VIP/DNS entries that are used for failover; keep higher TTLs for stable internal service records.
- Avoid overly large UDP DNS responses on tunnels (EDNS0 + TCP fallback) — enforce 1232B MTU path to prevent fragmentation over VXLAN/GRE.

NAT & connection tracking considerations:
- conntrack table sizing is critical at edge nodes. Default cloud images often undersize for 10k+ concurrent customers. Recommended conntrack max = (expected_conns_per_node * 2) + safety_margin. Monitor conntrack exhaustion alerts.
- For long-lived TLS sessions from customers, enable connection reuse on proxy to reduce new conntrack churn.

Security and compliance notes:
- All edge proxies should ship audit logs to a customer-indexed bucket with envelope encryption.
- KMS/HSM integration required for any TLS key material stored at rest or for certificate signing.
- Provide optional outbound allowlist templates for SOC customers, plus an emergency bypass policy that routes traffic to a hardened gateway under SRE control.

Monitoring / Runbook items (ops checklist snippets):
- Pre-upgrade:
  - Verify health checks for current proxies are green.
  - Capture baseline metrics (5m avg) for error rates, 95p latency, DNS error rate, conntrack usage.
  - Confirm terraform plan has no unexpected destroys.
- During upgrade:
  - Deploy canary proxy nodes with new image/version; attach to health-check group but do not move traffic until stable for 10m.
  - Shift 10% traffic via route/balancer to canary for 20m, observe metrics.
  - If stable, incrementally migrate remaining capacity in 20–30% steps.
- Post-upgrade validation:
  - Run smoke tests (http, dns, egress-ip check).
  - Confirm logs are forwarded and show no TLS errors or connection resets.

Known risks / gotchas (lessons learned):
- MTU mismatch across cloud VPN + on-prem can cause TCP stalls that look like proxy failures. Always validate end-to-end MTU and set MSS clamping on tunnels.
- Transparent interception breaks mTLS pinned certs. Only use for legacy apps after explicit customer signoff.
- Conntrack exhaustion manifests as sporadic 502s and is noisy to trace; we need better alerting at 70% table utilization.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Do we mandate edge static EIPs per-customer, or offer a shared pool with per-customer NAT port mapping? (tradeoffs: IP cost vs. application compatibility)
- FIPS mode for TLS at proxy – subset of customers require it; does that become an opt-in flag in TF module?
- Level of traffic inspection (L7) we store for debugging vs. privacy concerns.

Immediate TODOs (short term):
1) Draft customer-facing one-pager that explains: predictable egress IPs, proxy modes, required firewall rules on customer perimeter. Owner: Diego. ETA: 2025-10-15.
2) Add conntrack size var to edge module and expose recommended default. Owner: Evelyn. ETA: 2025-10-08.
3) Implement canary TF pipeline job that runs smoke validations automatically after terraform apply. Owner: Samir. ETA: 2025-10-20.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands
- Check conntrack usage (Linux): sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count ; sudo grep -i conntrack /proc/net/nf_conntrack
- Dump iptables redirect rules on gateway: sudo iptables -t nat -L PREROUTING -n -v
- Verify egress IP seen by external site: curl -sS https://ifconfig.co
- Check CoreDNS logs for stub-forward failures: kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=coredns

Notes on collaboration and references:
- Working branch: gh/rlw/private-edge-2025 (WIP)
- Related playbooks: see CON-1423 for network hardening baseline, and JIRA-PD-647 for previous incident postmortem.

If you are reviewing: please add inline comments for any assumptions you think are too prescriptive (esp. around TLS-intercept and customer data retention).
